sections.html:
Prices run low in Springfield and renters are common, which decides who shows up to buy. The typical owned home is worth $116,800 and the typical rent is $851. Owners hold 52.4% of the 24,650 households, and the median household earns $47,143. Springfield is the Clark County seat, roughly 45 miles west of Columbus and 25 miles northeast of Dayton. Headcount fell from 60,608 in 2010 to 58,662 in 2020, and the July 2025 estimate is 58,281.

Many buyers are investors planning to rent, so expect offers built around rental income and repair cost.

sections.h2: Older houses from the factory years
sections.html:
A lot of the housing goes back to the Champion City era, when factories employed much of the town. Population topped 82,000 in the 1960 census. Factory jobs then shrank and left many blocks of aging frame houses, so weigh repair spending against a modest sale price.

Some pockets are historic, such as the South Fountain Avenue Historic District and the Frank Lloyd Wright-designed Westcott House on East High Street. Houses nearby can attract a different kind of buyer, and it pays to ask the city before changing the outside of a house on a historic street.

Nearly half of Springfield households rent, and the city keeps a Rental Property Registry for those units. If you have a tenant, make sure your registration is current and this year's fee is paid before the house goes on the market.

Springfield rental registry fees
Rental typeAnnual registry fee
Single unit property$35
Two or more units in one building$25 per unit
Cap per owner and per LLC$750

Finishing a rental registration does not currently require the self-inspection checklist. Call 937-324-7385 with questions, and register through the online portal called City Works Online. Hold on to the receipt, since a buyer may want proof.

A separate Vacant Property Registry runs through HERA Property Registry. For an empty house, the city's Responsible Property Programming office can say if you must register and what it costs.

Visit 76 E. High Street, second floor, between 8 and 5. Complaints about an empty house tend to follow it into a sale, because boarded windows, tall grass or failing systems show up quickly in an inspection. That is one reason owners of vacant houses consider an as-is sale.

sections.h2: Which school district is your address in?
sections.html: Springfield City Schools cover most addresses. The Northeastern and Northwestern local districts take parts of the north, and Clark-Shawnee Local takes parts of the west, south and southeast. Confirm the district for your exact address before advertising it.

Clark County collects in two installments. Pay an installment late and a 5% penalty applies, climbing to 10% after a short window. The Treasurer, 937-521-1832, has current due dates and the balance for your parcel.

Bills go out 20 to 25 days before the due date, and a missing bill is no excuse for a late payment. An escrow program lets owners prepay monthly. At closing your title agent prorates the bill by days of ownership, so request that figure early.

sections.h2: Recording a deed in Clark County
sections.html:
R.C. 5301.25 sends a deed to the county where the land sits. The auditor indorses it after the grantee files a statement of value (R.C. 319.202), and the grantor pays the conveyance fee. On a residential rental, the indorsement also tells the grantee to file landlord details with the auditor, something investor buyers should expect.

Mention the Rental Property Registry to a rental buyer early. If they intend to keep renting, they will register under their own name after closing, and a clean record makes that easy.

sections.h2: Selling a house with a tenant in it
sections.html: Locate your registry receipt and confirm the current year is paid. Next, agree with the buyer on whether the tenant stays. An investor may welcome the lease, but an owner-occupant will want a move-out date in the contract. Share the lease and rent history at the outset. When title changes, the new owner registers the property, and the deed indorsement points them to the auditor's landlord filing.

Neighbors and inspectors notice an empty house. Ask the Responsible Property Programming office whether the address is on the Vacant Property Registry and whether complaints are open. Deal with what shows from the street first. If the problems go deeper than looks, an as-is buyer can spare you months of carrying costs. Leave utilities connected through the inspection, and have your title agent confirm no city charge is attached to the parcel.

1. Pull the parcel number and call the Treasurer to learn what is owed and when the next installment is due.
  2. Check city records for rental or vacant registration and any open code item.
  3. Choose a route: agent listing, sale on your own, or direct cash buyer.
  4. Sign a contract and let the title agent run the search.
  5. Have the deed and statement of value prepared, with the conveyance fee set aside from your proceeds.
  6. Review the settlement statement, including the tax proration, before you sign.

Bring a short list to the first call. Which county office will record the deed, and what will the conveyance fee come to on your price? Does the search show a rental or vacant registration, an unpaid tax installment or a city charge on the parcel? How will the tax bill be prorated, and will the statement of value be filed by the buyer or by the agent? If you hold a tenant's lease, ask whether it needs to be attached to the contract. Written answers are best, since you can hand them to any buyer who asks and compare offers on equal terms.

At a median value near $116,800, small costs matter more than they would in a pricier market. A registry fee, a repair bill and closing charges can add up against the sale price, so ask for every number before you accept an offer.

sections.h2: Is a cash sale the right fit?
sections.html:
It can be, if repairs would eat the gain from a retail listing. With a median value of $116,800, one big job such as a roof or furnace weighs heavily against the price, and a financed buyer may insist you do it first.

A direct buyer typically purchases as is, which suits a vacant or tenant-occupied house with open code items. Get two written offers, ask who covers closing costs, and review the settlement statement before the closing date.

faqs.q: Is there a city inspection before a Springfield house can be sold?
faqs.a: Ask the city's Responsible Property Programming office at 76 E. High Street whether your address has open code items or a vacant registration. Springfield's rental and vacant registries are the main property rules that touch a sale.

faqs.q: How much does Springfield charge to register a rental?
faqs.a: The annual fee is $35 for a single unit and $25 per unit in a building with two or more units, capped at $750 per owner and per LLC. Call 937-324-7385 with questions.

faqs.q: What is the late penalty on a Clark County tax bill?
faqs.a: An unpaid half draws a 5% penalty, which rises to 10% after a short grace window. Call the Treasurer at 937-521-1832 for the dates that apply.

faqs.q: Who pays the conveyance fee on a Springfield sale?
faqs.a: Under R.C. 319.202 the seller pays the fee, plus any county transfer tax the county has levied. The title company can quote the exact amount.

The South Fountain Avenue Historic District is one, and the Westcott House on East High Street was designed by Frank Lloyd Wright. Check with the city before planning exterior changes on a historic street.
